g.text: PagedAttention (vLLM): virtual memory for the KV cache
Explained on: session 10 PagedAttention / vLLM (notebook 10_pagedattention_vllm.ipynb) | Kwon et al. 2023, arXiv 2309.06180
1 The problem: contiguous max_len reservation vs paged blocks
Requests A-E (D has finished). Illustration: 1 cell = 1 allocation unit, 32 cells of GPU KV memory.
A 6 blocks, B 2, C 4, E 6 = 18 used, 14 free. E needs 6 blocks: ANY 6 free blocks work -> fits
Measured on older systems (paper): only 20.4-38.2% of KV memory held real token states
Paged: waste only in each sequence's last partial block -> under 4%
Internal fragmentation: slab sized for max_len, real output length unknown -> tail of every slab wasted
External fragmentation: free holes (5 + 3 cells) are not contiguous -> E (needs 6) cannot be placed
Over-reservation: a chat that stops after 40 tokens still pins a whole max_len slab
Slab of max_len = 8192 tokens on Llama-3-8B (128 KiB/token) = 1 GiB per request, whether or not it is used.
Same idea, same reason: stop requiring contiguity
physical KV block in GPU pool
allocate block when last one fills
Address translation, block_size = 16, token position p = 37, block_table[2] = 3:
Each sequence believes it owns one contiguous address space;
the block table hides where the pieces really live.
3 Logical blocks -> block table -> physical blocks
Illustration uses block_size = 4 so blocks stay readable (vLLM default is 16)
Logical order is contiguous; physical order is arbitrary and interleaved across sequences.
Only the LAST block can be partly empty -> waste <= block_size - 1 tokens per sequence.
Cost: one extra table lookup per block inside the attention kernel;
the block table must be available on the GPU.
4 Block-size math and the physical memory layout (Llama-3-8B, BF16)
L=32, H_kv=8, d_h=128, S=2 -> 128 KiB per token across all layers
KV per token, all layers : 2*L*H_kv*d_h*S = 2*32*8*128*2 = 131,072 B = 128 KiB
one block (16 tokens) : 16 x 128 KiB = 2 MiB (K and V, all 32 layers)
per layer per block : K[16,8,128] BF16 = 16*8*128*2 B = 32 KiB ; V same -> 64 KiB ; x32 layers = 2 MiB
max waste per sequence : (block_size - 1) tokens = 15 x 128 KiB = 1.875 MiB
chat of 500 tokens : reserve 8192 x 128 KiB = 1 GiB, use 500 x 128 KiB = 62.5 MiB -> 93.9% idle
paged : ceil(500/16) = 32 blocks = 64 MiB -> waste 12 tokens = 1.5 MiB
Small block: tiny waste, but big tables, poor memory-access efficiency, fine sharing granularity.
Large block: more waste in the last block and coarser prefix sharing. 16 is the vLLM default.
k_cache per layer: [num_blocks, block_size, H_kv, d_h] = [8580, 16, 8, 128] (v_cache identical)
zoom into block 3: block_size = 16 token slots
zoom into one slot: H_kv = 8 heads x d_h = 128 values (8*128*2 B = 2 KiB for K)
Pool size = KV budget / block bytes. Example: ~18 GB (~16.8 GiB) KV / 2 MiB = ~8,580 blocks
= ~137K tokens = ~16 sequences of 8K. Admission control is just counting free blocks.
5 Decode kernel: gather K/V blocks through the block table
H_q=32, H_kv=8, d_h=128, block_size=16; T=40 tokens -> ceil(40/16)=3 blocks (last holds 8)
s_j = q K_j^T / sqrt(d_h) q:[32,128] K_j:[16,8,128] s_j:[32,16] (q head h reads kv head h//4)
m_j = max(m_{j-1}, rowmax s_j) l_j = l_{j-1}*e^(m_{j-1}-m_j) + sum e^(s_j-m_j)
K, V = k_cache[p], v_cache[p] # [16, H_kv, d_h]
mask last block to T - 16*j valid slots
Same attention math; only the address calculation changed. Per-block online softmax
(FlashAttention style) means blocks need no gather-copy into a contiguous buffer.
Decode is memory-bound: every K/V byte is read once. Paging adds index loads, not FLOPs,
but the kernel must be written for non-contiguous access.
6 Copy-on-write with reference counts (parallel sampling, beam search)
Two samples of the same prompt (7 tokens, block_size 4 for readability). Blue = sample 1, orange = sample 2.
1 fork: both samples share the prompt
1. fork(n=2): both block tables point at the SAME prompt blocks
2. S1 writes slot 3 of P1, but ref(P1)=2 (shared) -> copy-on-write:
allocate P5, copy 3 slots, ref(P1) 2->1, ref(P5)=1, S1 -> P5
3. S2 writes slot 3 of P1: ref(P1)=1 -> private, write in place
P7 stays shared (ref=2) while both samples live
write while ref > 1 -> copy block, ref -= 1
write while ref == 1 -> in place, no copy
seq freed -> ref -= 1; at 0 block returns to pool
n=4 samples, 2,000-token prompt, 100 generated each (128 KiB/token):
shared + CoW : 2,000 + 4 x 100 = 2,400 token-states = 300 MiB (3.5x less)
(ignoring the one partly filled block per sample that CoW duplicates)
Beam search: beams share a long prefix; when a beam is pruned its blocks get
ref-1 and return to the pool at 0. Paper (Alpaca): memory saved 6.1-9.8% for
7 Prefix caching: 1000 users share a 2,000-token system prompt
Each full block is keyed by a hash chained to all previous tokens
A new request hashes its full 16-token blocks in order; each hit reuses the block (ref += 1), the first miss starts fresh compute.
no sharing : 1000 x 125 blocks x 2 MiB = 250,000 MiB ~ 244 GiB of identical K/V
shared : 125 x 2 MiB = 250 MiB once (+ small private tails)
prefill : the 2,000 prompt tokens are skipped for users 2..1000 -> TTFT = private suffix only
Only FULL blocks are hashed. Chained hash => a hit means identical prefix AND position.
Blocks with ref=0 stay cached and are evicted LRU when the pool needs space.
One changed token early (e.g. a timestamp in the system prompt) breaks the chain
for every block after it -> zero reuse. Keep the shared part first and byte-identical.
8 Preemption: when the block pool runs out
A running sequence needs a new block but none are free
running seq needs a new block
GPU blocks -> CPU RAM (swap_space) over PCIe
1 GiB seq @ ~25 GB/s ~ 43 ms out, again to resume
no recompute; costs CPU memory + PCIe time
drop the blocks, re-run prefill over
compute-bound; no PCIe, no CPU RAM
Paper: recompute cost is flat across block sizes; swap suffers with small blocks
(many tiny PCIe copies). At block sizes 16-64 the two are comparable.
Preemption is lost work. If it thrashes: cut max_num_seqs / max_model_len, raise
gpu_memory_utilization, use FP8 KV (S=1), or add GPUs.
9 What paging buys, and what it does NOT do
KV memory that holds real token states (paper numbers)
M_KV = 2 * L * B * T * H_kv * d_h * S <- paging does NOT change this
M_alloc = M_KV / utilisation : contiguous ~ M_KV / 0.2..0.38 ; paged ~ M_KV / 0.96+
paging attacks allocated/needed, not bytes per token
Throughput 2-4x vs FasterTransformer / Orca at similar latency: more sequences fit ->
bigger batches -> weights are reused across more tokens (decode is memory-bound).
Paging does not shrink the cache: 100K tokens of MHA is still 26.2 GB (toy config,
256 KiB/token). It only stops you wasting more on top of it.
Notebook 10 simulation (24 layers, 8 KV heads, d_h 128, 32 reqs, max_len 2048, block 16):
naive 6.00 GB vs paged 3.49 GB (41.9% less); waste 2.54 GB vs 24.38 MB.
Flags and defaults can differ between vLLM versions
tokens per KV block (waste vs table size, see 4)
GPU fraction vLLM may use: weights+KV pool+activations
longest sequence; lower = smaller worst-case need
cap on concurrent sequences in the batch
'fp8' -> S=1: block 2 MiB -> 1 MiB, 2x tokens per pool
CPU RAM per GPU for swapped-out blocks (see 8)
KV pool budget on a 40 GB A100, Llama-3-8B BF16:
0.9 x 40 = 36 GB - 16 GB weights - ~2 GB activations ~ 18 GB for KV
18 GB = 16.8 GiB / 2 MiB = ~8,580 blocks = ~137K tokens (fp8: ~17,160 blocks = ~274K tokens)
Tune order: fit weights, set gpu_memory_utilization, then block_size,
kv_cache_dtype and prefix caching; watch the 'GPU KV cache usage' metric.
Sources: Kwon et al., Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (SOSP 2023), arXiv 2309.06180; session 10 PagedAttention / vLLM.
